problems.description: Cognitive complexity +14 concentrated in handle_message/handler: nested validation branches for message types and payload shapes; could be decomposed into per-type handlers.
ClientRegistry guards every access with threading.RLock, but this is a single-threaded asyncio server where the lock is inert and misleads about concurrency model.
broadcast uses asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) but only ConnectionClosed prunes dead clients; other exceptions are silently swallowed and connections never get cleaned up.
Measured violations in test_app.py: test classes not PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE; production code is clean, but tests drift from the standard.

Full rewrite replaces the seeded Flask/sqlite structure (146 -> 171 lines) rather than layering onto its good seams; justified for a greenfield session 1 but discards all prior structure and backward-compat helpers.
No auth, rate limiting, or payload-size caps on inbound messages; any client can broadcast to all. Acceptable for tier-1 but worth noting.

strengths: Clean two-class decomposition: ClientRegistry (connection lifecycle) vs NotificationServer (messaging), each with a single responsibility.
Modern typing and style: from __future__ import annotations, dict[str, Any], timezone-aware timestamps.
Robust inbound validation that rejects malformed JSON and wrong payload shapes with explicit system errors.
Concurrent broadcast via asyncio.gather with per-connection exception handling instead of sequential awaits.
SonarQube confirms no new bugs and one fewer smell (+0 bugs, -1 smell), aligning with the clean production code.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured greenfield rewrite of app.py into an async WebSocket notification server that builds a sound registry/server design, matches the measured convention score of 0.82 (violations confined to the test file), and is net-better than the seed despite discarding the existing Flask structure.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +27 in handle_message: message-type dispatch, payload validation, and channel validation are all inline in one method, making the message handler harder to follow.

The inline set {"subscribe", "unsubscribe"} is built twice and channel validation (isinstance(str) and non-empty) is duplicated between the subscribe/unsubscribe branch and the general-message branch; extract a constant and a shared helper.
Convention score 0.82 (matches measured): 2 violations in test_app.py — a class not using PascalCase and a module-level constant not UPPER_CASE.

strengths: Channel state is co-located in ClientRegistry under the existing threading.RLock, and remove() prunes empty channels on disconnect, preventing stale-subscriber leaks.
Reuses the existing send/message/broadcast idioms and system-error pattern rather than introducing a parallel delivery protocol.
New /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers endpoints follow the established process_request pattern, with unquote() correctly handling URL-encoded channel names.
channel_snapshot defensively filters subscribers no longer in _clients, so a stale registry entry cannot crash delivery.
Ships tests for the new behavior via a fetch_json helper, keeping coverage aligned with the feature.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-consistent channel feature that extends the existing registry/broadcast architecture with proper lock discipline and disconnect cleanup; only caveats are a +27 cognitive-complexity bump in the message handler and two minor test-file convention violations matching the measured 0.82.

problems.description: json.loads(data) in _subscriber_worker has no exception handling — a single malformed payload kills the delivery task permanently (only the ready event is set in finally, no retry/reconnect loop), silently halting all message delivery.
MessageStore.add()/list() perform synchronous sqlite3 I/O (check_same_thread=False + threading.Lock) inside the asyncio event loop via _publish, blocking all WebSocket handling on disk writes.

Integration grows app.py by +417/-45 lines with cognitive complexity +54 (per SonarQube); subscriber task + ready event + lifecycle lock add non-trivial lifecycle state to NotificationServer ahead of the Session 4 transport extraction.
Convention score 0.82 with 2 violations in test_app.py: class should be PascalCase and module-level constant should be UPPER_CASE (per measurement).

strengths: Design matches the Session 3 spec closely: Redis pub/sub backbone, SQLite MessageStore, REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL config, and paginated GET /messages.
Correct async lifecycle handling — _start_subscriber/_stop_subscriber use a lifecycle lock plus a ready event to avoid subscribing races.
Elegant single-instance fallback in _publish: delivers directly when no Redis is configured, preserving existing behavior.
Clean Redis key namespacing (notifications:messages/clients/channels, per-client/channel keys) that is collision-safe across server instances.
Consistent type hints, docstrings, and the generic close_async_resource helper for sync/async close symmetry.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid spec-aligned Redis/SQLite integration that preserves existing routing behavior with a sensible fallback, but ships with real technical debt from unhandled subscriber failures and blocking DB I/O in the event loop.

problems.description: WebSocketTransport reaches into NotificationServer private methods (_add_client, _remove_client, _stop_subscriber, handle_message, send), coupling the transport to server internals instead of a defined seam; the bidirectional bind() plus private-method calls is a leaky abstraction.

BaseTransport.broadcast() contract leaks WebSocket-specific semantics: it returns disconnected client IDs and the server drives cleanup via ConnectionClosed-based results, tying the ABC's return contract to one transport's failure model rather than transport-internal lifecycle handling.

handler() is defined only on the concrete WebSocketTransport, not the ABC; NotificationServer falls back to getattr(self.transport, 'handler', None) duck-typing, undermining the interface contract that a future transport must implement.

The 2 measured violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants) are in test_app.py, which the shown app.py diff does not touch; if pre-existing, the 0.82 convention score overstates the debt introduced by this refactor.

strengths: Introduces a clean BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport implementation that genuinely decouples notification handling from the connection protocol and enables future SSE/gRPC backends.
Moves the direct/channel/broadcast targeting logic and failure handling out of NotificationServer into the transport, reducing server complexity (cognitive complexity +4 only for a +116-line change).
TRANSPORTS registry with env-driven selection (TRANSPORT) and an explicit ValueError on unsupported transports is a clean, testable seam.
Preserves the existing public surface (client registry, message flow, handler lifecycle) while adding optional transport injection to the constructor for dependency-injection-friendly testing.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that extracts a transport abstraction from the notification server, but ships leaky seams — private-method coupling and WebSocket-specific semantics in the ABC — that should be tightened before a second transport lands.

problems.description: The /history endpoint validation is written as a bare try/raise ValueError block with multiple boolean conditions, contributing the measured +25 cognitive complexity for a parsing task that could be decomposed.

Rate limiting is applied before message parsing and to all message types (including subscribe/unsubscribe and malformed messages), so invalid traffic consumes the client quota and the counter increments are never short-circuited by a check-then-act.

Measured violations reference test_app.py (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants) but the AST diff shows +0 files changed, indicating these naming issues are pre-existing test-file debt rather than introduced by this commit.

strengths: Message history uses cursor-style pagination with a has_more flag and a limit+1 fetch, a clean pattern for incremental sync.
Timestamp handling is correct: requires timezone-aware ISO input, normalizes to UTC before querying, and stores consistent strings.
Rate limiting uses the idiomatic Redis INCR + conditional EXPIRE fixed-window pattern with a matching notifications:rate-limit key namespace.
Cleanup worker follows the codebase's async task lifecycle conventions: double-checked start under _lifecycle_lock, cooperative cancellation via asyncio.Event, and CancelledError handling.
Configuration respects the existing env-var + constructor-injection pattern (TRANSPORT, DATABASE_URL) via _positive_int_setting with clear validation errors.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit (history endpoint, TTL retention, rate limiting) that fits the existing config, Redis-keying, and async-task patterns with no measured bugs or duplications; the only real cost is localized parsing complexity (+25 cognitive complexity) and pre-existing test-file naming violations that keep the convention score at 0.82.

compounding_issues: Session 1 completely discarded the seed codebase (a Flask todo API with a notification stub) in favor of a greenfield rewrite, so no seed structure or code survived to anchor or constrain later sessions

Session 4's transport abstraction (BaseTransport/TRANSPORT env) shipped with zero new tests — the plugin seam is verified only indirectly by the pre-existing suite, and no dedicated custom-transport test was added

The modern-vs-legacy websockets HTTP API compatibility shim introduced in Session 3 (`not isinstance(path, str)` branching) persists and accumulates complexity across process_request/_json_response in every later session
Session 5's rate limiting silently no-ops when Redis is not configured (returns True), and the message TTL cleanup worker only fires once per 86400s, making both behaviors hard to observe or test
A test timing race noted in Session 1 was never explicitly resolved and its test persisted unchanged through the story
key_decisions: Session 1: greenfield rewrite of the seed into a standalone asyncio WebSocket notification server with a JSON envelope protocol (type/payload/channel) and a client_id handshake over a system message

Session 2: backward-compatible channel subscription model (subscribe/unsubscribe message types, per-channel routing in ClientRegistry) that preserved global broadcast when channel is omitted and restored legacy error text after a validation refactor

Session 3: opt-in Redis pub/sub fan-out across multiple server instances plus Redis-backed client/channel metadata and a thread-safe SQLite MessageStore, all gated on REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL so prior behavior was preserved without Redis
Session 4: pluggable transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport, TRANSPORT env selection) while retaining compatibility attributes server.clients/handler/process_request

Session 5: cross-cutting operations layered on sessions 3-4 — Redis sliding-minute rate limiting, a daily SQLite message TTL cleanup worker, and a /history endpoint with timezone-aware `since` filtering and has_more pagination
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions, with the codebase maturing from a single-class, single-process server into a layered architecture (MessageStore, ClientRegistry, BaseTransport, NotificationServer) while test count grew from 5 to 13 and the full suite passed at every checkpoint. Each session extended the previous one cleanly — channels built on the session-1 protocol, Redis/SQLite integration on channels, the transport refactor on integration, and rate limiting/cleanup/history on the Redis-SQLite foundation — so there was no backtracking or rework. The only flat spot was Session 4's refactor, which introduced abstraction without adding new tests, though it preserved behavior and left the codebase in a better-pluggable state that Session 5 capitalized on.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, textbook incremental build in which every session layered cleanly onto the prior one and the codebase evolved into a modular, integration-tested notification platform — held back only by the wholesale abandonment of the seed and a refactor session that added a plugin seam without any new tests.
